questions.q: What is a pull request, fundamentally?
options: A GitHub feature: a request to merge one branch into another that opens a space for discussion, checks, and review before the merge happens
A Git command that merges branches automatically with no review
A way to permanently delete a branch
A built-in part of Git itself, required before any merge
questions.explain: Pull requests are a GitHub (not Git) concept — git merge doesn't require one; PRs add a review checkpoint on top of Git.

questions.q: What does GitHub's "Compare & pull request" banner offer to do?
options: Immediately delete the pushed branch
Open the comparison between your recently pushed branch and the base branch, as the start of opening a PR
Automatically merge the branch with no review
Download the repository as a ZIP file
questions.explain: That banner appears after a push and offers a shortcut straight into opening a pull request comparing the two branches.

questions.q: On a pull request's tab bar, where does the actual code diff and code review happen?
options: The Conversation tab
The Commits tab
The Checks tab
The Files changed tab
questions.explain: Files changed shows the actual diff, which is where inline review comments get attached to specific lines.

questions.q: What is the "base branch" in a pull request?
options: The branch containing your proposed changes
A branch that gets automatically deleted after the PR
The branch being merged into, usually main
The very first commit in the repository
questions.explain: The base branch is the target of the merge; the compare branch is the one carrying your changes.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why are small, focused pull requests generally better than large ones covering many unrelated changes?
options: GitHub technically limits PRs to a small number of files
They're faster and easier to review thoroughly, and much easier to revert cleanly if something turns out to be wrong
Small PRs don't require any review at all
There is no practical difference in review quality
questions.explain: A focused PR is easier for a reviewer to actually evaluate, rather than rubber-stamping an overwhelming change.
